nodes.label: Employee and user full separation
nodes.source_location: Topic 10 origin / Where this comes from
nodes.rationale: Option 1 (full separation) was chosen over leaving user untouched or letting user double as the employee table, because the office's people would otherwise live in two tables, and because making login code responsible for always excluding password-less rows is easy to get wrong later.

nodes.label: employee table
nodes.rationale: One row per person in the office whether or not they log in. Holds name, position_title, position_short_form, org_unit_fk, birth_date, sex, civil_status, tenure_status, employment_status. No employee number, because COS and Job Order staff hold no plantilla item so the column would be empty for much of the office.

nodes.label: user table (login only)
nodes.rationale: Holds only sign-in facts: username, password_hash, role_fk, account_status, must_change_password, failed_login_attempts, locked_until, last_login_at. Name fields moved to employee because a person has one name whether or not they sign in.

nodes.label: role_fk stays on the login
nodes.rationale: "Role in the office" is position_title on employee; "role in the app" is a permission bundle. On employee, role_fk would be empty for most of the office and every reader would first have to check whether the person even has a login — a check easy to forget.

nodes.label: One employee, one login (unique employee_fk)
nodes.rationale: user.employee_fk is required and unique. Required because the sidebar name lives on the employee row, so a login with no employee is a login with no name and every screen would need an extra branch. Unique because the system records who did what, and two accounts for one human make "who changed this?" unanswerable.

nodes.label: Super admin handover is a new account, not a shared password
nodes.source_location: Topic 4 — The super admin is an employee too
nodes.rationale: Passing one admin login down between post-holders destroys attribution. Instead a second super admin user is created and the old one deactivated; RBAC already allows several holders, refuses to reach zero active holders, and warns at two-to-one.

nodes.label: Four distinct status columns
nodes.rationale: employment_status, civil_status and tenure_status on employee plus account_status (renamed from status) on user. The same word must never be reused across the two tables or whoever writes a query later reads the wrong one; "separated" unavoidably appears in two of them with different meanings.

nodes.label: tenure_status (seven CSC categories)
nodes.rationale: permanent, temporary, casual, coterminous, contractual, cos, job_order. COS and JO sit apart because those people are engaged under a separate joint circular rather than CSC rules. `substitute` was excluded because the office never fills a post while its holder is on long leave. Displayed as "Type of appointment" rather than "Tenure".

nodes.label: employment_status kept at active/separated
nodes.rationale: Recording why somebody left (retirement, resignation, dismissal) overlaps with a personnel system; EMS is an environmental management system, so that belongs in an HR system if the agency ever gets one.

nodes.label: Two admin pages: Employees and Users
nodes.rationale: One dialog for both records would ask for fourteen things; the two lists are different sizes so a merged page would carry empty account columns; and keeping the staff list current is clerical work while creating a login decides who may do what. Accepted cost: hiring somebody who needs a login means visiting two pages.

nodes.label: admin:view_employees and admin:manage_employees
nodes.rationale: A new `employees` submodule in PERMISSION_DEFS so a clerk can keep the staff list current without also being able to create accounts and assign roles. The Users page still lists employees without needing view_employees, since the key guards the page rather than reading names elsewhere.

nodes.label: sync-permissions backfills the super-admin role
nodes.source_location: Topic 6 — The missing step was added
nodes.rationale: The super-admin role is frozen in the role editor, so a new admin:* key it does not already hold could never be granted through the interface. Re-normalizing does not help because implication only runs upward. The script now finds that role by the permission admin:manage_roles rather than by name, inserts missing admin:* keys in one transaction, names what it added, and skips cleanly on a fresh database.

nodes.label: Duplicate employee check
nodes.rationale: Exact match on first name, last name and birth date refuses the save; a birth-date match with a different name, or a name match where one record has no birth date, only warns and lets the admin decide. Written once in duplicate-check.ts and run both live in the dialog and in the server actions, which cannot be bypassed. Edits run the same check, excluding the record being edited.

nodes.label: Birth date as the identity anchor
nodes.source_location: Topic 7a — the birth date is the anchor, not the name
nodes.rationale: A birth date never changes: not on marriage, not on rehire, and it is the same for any tenure. An earlier system branched on the sex field to allow for a changed surname, but sex can be mistyped and then the whole check silently behaves differently, so that branch was dropped. The form and the server require a birth date while the column stays nullable, which keeps the "one record has no birth date" rule from being dead code.

nodes.label: Bring this person back (reinstate)
nodes.rationale: An exact match on somebody who has left offers reinstatement inside the form rather than a bare refusal, because otherwise an admin changes a spelling to force the save and creates the duplicate the check exists to prevent. It also applies the typed position, section, tenure and civil status, since people rarely return to the same job, and the alert lists each change as old to new.

nodes.label: Sign-in refuses anyone no longer employed
nodes.rationale: Option C beat switching the account off at the same moment (option B) because B leaves a gap: an admin could switch the account back on without touching the employment record. validateSessionToken deletes a session whose employee is not active, the login joins employee and refuses before looking at account status, and the Users page shows a "Person has left" badge so a dead account never reads plain Active.

nodes.label: endSessionsForEmployee helper
nodes.rationale: Shared by the `separate` action and by `update` when the edit is what marks somebody as having left; the editor was the second way in and would otherwise have left the person signed in.

nodes.label: employee_history table (versions)
nodes.rationale: One row per version of a person's name, position title and short form, with valid_from and valid_until. Documents point at a version rather than at the person, so a marriage or a promotion cannot rewrite paperwork already filed. employee keeps its own copy as the current value so an ordinary lookup stays one read, and both tables are written in one transaction by one function.

nodes.label: Version date rules (valid_until is inclusive)
nodes.rationale: valid_until is the last day the version was still correct. A printed field changing closes the old version yesterday and opens the new one today, or a document filed today would match the same person twice. Separation closes the open version today, which is what removes the person from later documents. A version begun today is corrected in place, and one closed earlier today is reopened, because a version covering only today cannot be what any document points at — the reopen rule was a bug found in testing.

nodes.label: backfill-employee-history script (2000-01-01 start)
nodes.rationale: Safe to run twice because it skips anybody who already has a version. Backfilled versions start at 2000-01-01 rather than the run date because paper is always typed in after it was signed, so a slip filed last week must still find its signatories; Topic 8 of the signatory document already ruled out reports for periods before go-live.

nodes.label: position_short_form
nodes.source_location: Topic 9 — Why the short form is allowed to be empty
nodes.rationale: The boxes on the paper forms are small, so documents print "AO-I/Supply Officer" rather than "Administrative Officer I (Supply Officer)"; no rule worth trusting derives one from the other, so somebody types it once. Nullable, because a non-null column would have made the backfill impossible without inventing values. The rule that it must be present belongs to the document that prints it, which must refuse to print rather than leave a blank line.

nodes.label: employee_history cascades where everything else restricts
nodes.rationale: With restrict every employee would become undeletable the moment the backfill gave them a first version, breaking the delete button even for somebody added by mistake. The protection arrives from the other side instead: a document holds a history row with restrict, so deleting that employee fails at the cascade and the person stays.

nodes.label: drizzle-kit push is unsafe on this project
nodes.source_location: Topic 9 — Applying it to the database
nodes.rationale: Asked to add employee_history it also offered to repair earlier drift, and its way of adding a NOT NULL rule to a MySQL column is to TRUNCATE the table first; with --force it attempted that on employee and was saved only by the foreign key from user. Schema changes are applied as plain SQL instead.

nodes.label: Correcting an entry versus recording a change
nodes.rationale: A typing mistake was never correct so filed documents should be repaired; a marriage or promotion was correct at the time so old documents must keep the old value. The user replaced a question-at-save-time design with two separate entry points, so the button pressed already says which case it is and nothing has to be inferred or asked halfway through a save. A correction touches only the version being looked at; a closed version is corrected deliberately from the history panel.

nodes.label: employee_history_correction log
nodes.rationale: Editing a version in place silently changes every document using it, which is the case the user wanted attributable, so each changed field is logged with who did it and when. Held in the database only for now.

nodes.label: Name and position history sheet
nodes.rationale: A shadcn-svelte sheet rather than a dialog, because the content is a list of unknown length and is read far more often than written. Named from four plain candidates: "Name history" promised less than the screen shows, "Change history" does not say change of what, "Employee history" sounds like hire and leave dates, and Service Record is a real CSC document carrying salary and appointment data this system does not store. Entries are fetched when the panel opens rather than with the page.

nodes.label: Add name or position change dialog
nodes.rationale: Door 2: closes the open version and starts a new one, the "record a change that happened" path, opened from the employees table row menu.

nodes.label: Correct this entry dialog
nodes.rationale: Door 3: edits one existing version in place from the history sheet, carrying the warning headed "This corrects what is already filed".

nodes.label: No separate admin:correct_employees key, for now
nodes.rationale: Adding the key would take away an ability roles already have on day one, against a small risk in an office with two logins where every repair is already attributed. Adding it later is one PERMISSION_DEFS entry and two guards, while removing a key roles depend on is the harder direction. Decided by Claude, not the user, and recorded so it can be overruled.

nodes.label: create-admin.ts asks instead of inventing a person
nodes.rationale: The script used to write a placeholder "Admin User" employee with position System Administrator and tenure Permanent, which contradicted the whole argument for requiring the employee link and left a fake row in the Employees list. It already interviews whoever runs it for a username, so the real name, position, appointment type and birth date join the same run, and it opens the first history entry with its own SQL.

nodes.label: Lockout through the Employees page
nodes.rationale: Sign-in asks two questions (is the account active, does this person still work here) while every other part of the system asks only the first, so the state "account active, employee separated" locks somebody out while the rest of the system thinks the account is fine. The Employees page gains the guards the Users page already has: no separating yourself, and no leaving zero super admins who can actually sign in. The password reset script also reports success on an account that cannot be used.

nodes.label: Mark as employed (undoing a mistaken separation)
nodes.rationale: Separating closes the open version and reinstating opens a new one, so the pair is not an undo: the history shows a break in service that never happened and documents dated inside the gap find nobody. The missing operation reopens the closed version instead. One neutral menu item, mirroring "Mark as no longer employed", then a dialog asks whether the person really left or the record was a mistake — a question anybody can answer without being taught, unlike the correct-versus-change split in Topic 10. "Mark as employed again" was rejected because "again" answers the question the dialog is about to ask.
